post.author: chris
post.text: I'm starting this series because I wish I had something like this when I was trying to understand startup roles myself. Before we get into it, you might reasonably be asking: who is writing this? TLDR: After graduating, I was as an early-stage VC investor at @panachevc who then left to join @trynationgraph. a Series A startup backed by @Menloventures to do growth/marketing. Seven months later, I got promoted, helped bring in hundreds of thousands of dollars in closed-won deals, generated millions in pipeline, and was recently featured by Clay as a GTM engineer to watch. This isn't to boast but to show you that anything is possible and you can also break into a startup too as someone non-technical. I'm still figuring it out but I ought to share some lessons on the way. In this series: I’m going to try to show you exactly what I would do if I had to start from zero again: Which roles I’d target and which exist. Which kinds of companies I’d go after. How I’d get their attention, and how I’d turn that attention into a job. Let's start with the basics and what roles exist. At most startups you should probably be either building or selling This is an oversimplification, but I think it's a useful way to think about most early-stage startups generally. At the beginning, a startup really needs to do two things: build something people want and figure out how to get people to buy it. If you're an engineer, the first path is fairly obvious. You can help build the product. If you're non-technical and early in your career, I think you should try to get as close as possible to the second. Help the company get customers. This doesn't mean every non-technical person needs to become part of the GTM team within the startup. As startups get into later stages, there are obviously many other important roles: account management, product managers, finance, operations, recruiting, chiefs of staff, and so on. But many of those roles become easier to break into once you have a few years of experience and a clearer skill set. This guide is specifically for someone coming out of school or with less than two years of experience who doesn't have much of a track record yet. At that stage, I think one of the easiest ways to make yourself valuable is to work on something the company cares about every single day: revenue. That could mean directly selling the product. It could mean generating pipeline for the sales team. It could mean creating content that brings people to the website. It could mean improving SEO, running events, making videos, building outbound campaigns, or automating parts of the entire process. The titles for these jobs can get confusing very quickly: sales, growth, community, marketing, demand gen, SDR, BDR, GTM engineering. When I was first looking at startup jobs, half of these sounded like completely different careers. But it's actually quite simple if you break it down. So what actually falls under GTM? The easiest way to simplify it is to think about it is to think about it is outbound and inbound GTM. Outbound means you go find the customer. You figure out which companies should buy your product, find the right people inside those companies, and try to start a conversation with them: Cold calling and cold email are the obvious examples, but it also includes prospecting, account research, list building, LinkedIn outreach, writing sequences, and all the work that goes into turning a company you've never spoken to into a sales opportunity. If you see an SDR or BDR role, this is generally the world you're entering. Inbound works in the opposite direction. Instead of going out and finding each customer, you're creating things that make potential customers find you. This is where a lot of what we traditionally call marketing sits: Writing content, making videos, working with UGC creators, publishing blog posts, improving the website, building landing pages, working on SEO/AEO, running events, creating case studies, and generally finding ways to get more of the right people interested in what you're building. If you see a founding Marketer, community, social media manager this is generally the direction you will be entering. Now the title "Growth" is no different, it just means you're living somewhere between the lines above or all of it at once depending on the company. More recently, there is another layer that sits across both of these: GTM engineering. Whatever you want to call it! You don't have to be an engineer to be a GTM engineer The name makes this role sound more intimidating than it is. At a basic level, this type of "engineering" work is using software, data, AI, and automation to make sales and marketing more effective. Contrary to popular belief you do not need to come from an engineering background or degree to do this role. Maybe your sales team is manually researching 100 accounts. You build a workflow that can research 10,000 (this is what @trynationgraph does if you sell to the government). Maybe you're manually finding the right person at every company before sending them an email. You create a system that automatically sends cold emails to website visitors. Maybe your marketing team is doing the same repetitive research every week. You automate their work. A few years ago, doing a lot of this would have required significantly more engineering help. That's changing quickly. Tools like @Clay and AI coding agents like @Claudeai have made it possible for people who aren't software engineers to build surprisingly sophisticated things. But there's an important distinction here: Not being an engineer doesn't mean you should be afraid of technical things. You don't need to learn how to build production level ready code. But you should know what GitHub is. You should understand the basics of pushing and pulling changes. You should be comfortable opening the terminal and using simple bash commands like cd and ls. You should understand your local file system and have a rough idea of how API/MCPs work. AI can increasingly handle the implementation. Your job is to understand the problem well enough to tell it what you want, give it the right context, recognize when it gives you something bad, and steer it toward something better. That's where taste becomes important. title: Three reminders for when life feels overwhelming
tldr: Shaan Puri shares an email to a friend: life is seasonal, choose response over reaction, and control only the controllables.
note: @ShaanVP: My friend came over yesterday and I could tell something was wrong. - his mom has a scary health issue - his own health has felt off for months (docs keep saying 'everything looks fine', but it's not) - wife is panicking googling his symptoms and seeing scary stuff On top of…

post.author: Shaan Puri
post.text: My friend came over yesterday and I could tell something was wrong. - his mom has a scary health issue - his own health has felt off for months (docs keep saying 'everything looks fine', but it's not) - wife is panicking googling his symptoms and seeing scary stuff On top of that, he felt like he was underperforming at work. None of these things, by themselves, were crushing. But all of them at once? Overwhelmed. And hte worst part of feeling overwhelmed isn't the feeling. it's feeling ashamed for feeling that way. Today, I sent him this email: Hey man— I’ve been thinking about our conversation. There are three things I want you to remember. 1. Remember: life is seasonal. When you’re in a bad season, your brain does this funny thing where it assumes, This is just life now. It isn’t. You’ve had seasons where everything was clicking. You’ve also had storms that, at the time, felt like they’d never end. But they did. This one will too. 2. Remember: there’s only one decision to make. When you have 1,000 things hitting you at once, it’s easy to get overwhelmed and overthink it. In reality, you only have 1 decision to make: Am I going to have a common reaction or uncommon response? “Reactions” are automatic. Impulsive. “Responses” are choices. You get to choose how you respond to the situation. When we’re in the gym lifting - those last 2 reps when our arms are shaking, there’s a reaction of “sh*t this is hard” and so you break form and rush it. But the response is to choose poise. Deep breath. Remind yourself these last few reps are where all the gains happen. So you slow down and finish strong. Most guys in your position will have a common reaction: You feel overwhelmed, then you feel sorry for yourself. You start avoiding the things you know you need to do, then you feel guilty because you’re avoiding them, which makes you even more overwhelmed. Round and round you go. You don’t need to have perfect responses 100% of the time. But if you can switch from a ‘common reaction’ to an ‘uncommon response’ 50-75% of the time, that changes everything. Life is either happening to you or for you. 3. Remember: control the controllables. The serenity prayer says: Grant me the serenity to accept the things I cannot change, the courage to change the things I can, and the wisdom to know the difference. A lot of your suffering right now is coming from trying to play God. You want to control your mom’s health, your health, your wife’s anxiety, what happens at work, and how everyone feels about all of it. You can’t. That’s not your job. Your job is to control the controllables: your actions. Fly back home. Show up with a cheerful attitude. Make the appointments with the doctors. Get good sleep. Control what you can control. Everything else you either let go of, or get dragged by. This experience is happening whether you like it or not. You’re going through the tunnel. The question isn’t whether you go through it. The question is how you go through it. Go through it well. —shaan P.S. go for a run I don’t have great ideas when I’m depressed. The first thing to do is change your state of mind. The fastest way to do that is an intense physical thing. Go sprint. Do pushups. Take a freezing shower. Get outside. Change the body first, then think. And when you come up with one good thing to do, do it immediately. Action creates momentum, and momentum makes the next action easier.

tldr: Isaiah Granet nearly fired a Bland SDR who ignored outbound but quietly closed the two biggest deals, arguing workers should chase outsized wins over busywork.

note: @zaygranet: I hired one of our first employees at Bland to be an SDR. For several months he did basically none of that, and I was working out how to let him go. What I didn't know was that he'd been quietly working three accounts himself. He'd decided that closing those three mattered more…

post.author: Isaiah Granet
post.text: I hired one of our first employees at Bland to be an SDR. For several months he did basically none of that, and I was working out how to let him go. What I didn't know was that he'd been quietly working three accounts himself. He'd decided that closing those three mattered more than the outbound I kept hounding him about. Then he closed our biggest deal, and then the next one (Everyone at Bland knows exactly who I'm talking about. He knows I'm writing this. He has not asked to read it first, which is very on brand.) He hasn't had a task assigned to him in a long time. He does more or less what he wants, and I'm fine with that. He figured out before I did that he'd rather catch the snitch than score hoops. He found his golden snitch I. The Rules In Quidditch, a goal is worth ten points. Catching the snitch is worth a hundred and fifty and ends the match. Fifteen goals at once, and no time for the other team to answer. Unless you're far enough behind, you've won. There are results like that at work. For an AE, there's a deal big enough to make the year's quota on its own. Close it and the question of whether you'll hit quota is settled. For an engineer, it might be cutting the cost of running the product enough to make the business profitable. For an FDE, getting a customer to expand from one team to the whole company. These aren't just unusually productive weeks. They're results big enough to settle the thing you were trying to accomplish. That's your snitch. You should know what it is. II. It Looks Like Work The chaser is visibly busy all match. The seeker is circling, looking, apparently doing nothing. If you didn't know the rules, you'd assume the chaser was the one earning their keep. That's why my hire looked like a problem. Outbound is countable. You can put it in a spreadsheet and review it Monday. Three accounts he was quietly working didn't show up anywhere until they closed. I wanted customers. I'd assigned him outbound because I thought that was how he'd help us get them. He'd found another way, and I was so busy checking whether he was doing what I'd asked that I nearly missed it. It's easy to make this mistake from either side. As an employee, you can spend your whole week responding to requests. There's always another one, and someone is usually pleased when you finish it. You can go a long time without asking what all this work is supposed to add up to. The snitch may never appear on your task list. Whoever writes the list may not have seen it either. III. It Feels Unfair Suppose you've been working hard, doing everything you're asked. A colleague seems to ignore half the assignments, spends months on something you barely understand, and then gets the praise and the freedom. You put in more hours. Why do they get to choose their own work? That reaction makes sense if you think the rewards are supposed to measure effort. We know what our own work cost us. We remember the weekends and the problems that ran long. We want those counted. But a hundred and fifty points are a hundred and fifty points. They don't become worth less because someone else worked harder for ten. If an engineer saves the company a million dollars in a month, spending six months on a feature doesn't necessarily make the feature more valuable. The effort was real. So was the million dollars. This is easier to understand when you're the customer. If someone fixes your problem in an hour, you don't wish they'd taken a week. It's also easier when you remember you're on the same team. You wouldn't want a teammate to pass up the snitch because you'd spent the afternoon scoring goals. You'd want them to catch it. And once someone has found and caught it a few times, giving them freedom is a fairly practical decision. They've shown they can identify something worth doing without waiting for you to assign it. You want them to keep doing that. IV. Finding It In Quidditch, you know what you're looking for. At work, figuring that out can be the hardest part. Try finishing this sentence: if I accomplish _____ in the next six months, it will be obvious I've done an exceptional job. The answer should describe a result. “Work on infrastructure” doesn't. “Cut the cost to serve each customer in half without hurting reliability” does. Then check whether that result would matter as much as you think. Halving an expense that barely costs anything isn't a snitch. A useful place to look is at something important that keeps failing to happen. A customer likes the product but won't expand. They have a long list of feature requests, so you keep building features. But perhaps they need a second department using the product before they can approve a bigger contract. Finishing the first department's list won't get you there. Learning that changes what you should do tomorrow. It may also make the work you've already done worth much more. Talk to the people who depend on the result. Find out what is actually stopping them. Before spending six months on your explanation, see whether you can test it in a week. And don't assume the snitch will be glamorous. It might be getting a deployment to work, fixing one persistent source of customer churn, or having a conversation you've been avoiding. What makes it the snitch is what happens when you catch it. V. Winning You can win on goals. An AE who makes quota through twenty small deals has made quota. Someone who does the ordinary work exceptionally well, month after month, can contribute an enormous amount. But you have to know whether the goals you're scoring are enough. You can be ahead for most of a Quidditch match and still lose when the other team catches the snitch. Being busy all afternoon doesn't change the final score. The same problem shows up in a company that keeps signing customers and keeps losing them. Sales may be doing everything right. Everyone may be working hard. But if customers leave faster than you can replace them, doing more of the same won't be enough. Someone has to go after the reason they leave. You can lose by never looking for the thing that would decide the game. You can also lose by doing nothing else. Some people spend months “working on strategy” without getting close to an actual result. My hire was working three accounts. He had customers to convince and deals to close. Calling yourself a seeker doesn't put points on the board. And even a catch isn't always enough. Krum catches the snitch in the World Cup final and Bulgaria still loses because they're too far behind (and yes, I said books. If you've only seen the movies reconsider your life choices). If pursuing one customer costs you the rest of your business, closing them doesn't make it a good trade. You should know your snitch even if you decide to keep scoring goals. You should have some idea of what would be worth dropping the next assignment for. Otherwise, it's easy to spend all your time on the work that arrives and never pursue the result that would make the biggest difference. I nearly fired someone for making that decision better than I had. I haven't assigned him a task in a long time. I still have plenty of things I'd like done. He's not going to do them. That's fine with me, because he's my seeker. Blandly,

post.author: Alex
post.text: Hi, I'm Alex, cofounder at @relate_studio. In this tutorial, I'll walk you through how we design brand mascots with AI: finding first concepts in Krea, refining the best direction in Nano Banana 2, generating new poses and angles, and turning everything into a concept you can scale. A lot of brand designers shy away from projects like this because mascot design feels like something that requires strong illustration or 3D skills. In reality, AI tools alone can already get you to a result strong enough to present to a client and detailed enough for a motion designer to use as reference for a full 3D build. For the sake of this article, I will show you how we made the following mascot for the Yoru project 1. Gather references and define the mascot Start by collecting references in Figma and deciding what kind of personality, proportions, materials, and overall style you want. For this mascot, we wanted a stylized 3D anthropomorphic character. Most of my references were 3D, but I also included a few 2D examples. One of them actually had more personality than any of the 3D references. Don't limit yourself to references that look exactly like the final result. Mixing different styles can lead to more interesting generations. 2. Generate rough concepts in Krea For early exploration, we used Krea. It's convenient because you can access multiple AI models from a single interface instead of constantly jumping between tools. Upload a few references and start generating rough concepts. At this stage, the goal isn't to get a perfect mascot. You're just looking for interesting shapes, proportions, clothes, expressions, and personalities worth developing further. Prompt: "3D stylized mascot character, anthropomorphic rabbit, cocky and playful attitude, standing pose, wearing dark bomber jacket, soft rubber/plastic material look, rounded friendly proportions, big expressive eyes, thick fluffy tail, clean isolated character on dark background, front three-quarter view, high detail, centered composition." Pro-tip: You can also let Krea generate the prompt for you by dragging a reference image into the prompt field. 3. Pick the strongest base Then, after multiple generations, select the best result. Don't worry about small mistakes yet! The version I picked had a strange artifact on the pant leg and inconsistent color on the jacket, but the overall anatomy and proportions were strong. At this stage, it's much more important to get the silhouette, personality, and proportions right than to polish every detail. 4. Refine the mascot in Nano Banana 2 Next, take the strongest concept into Nano Banana 2 and clean it up. You can fix textures, colors, clothing details, backgrounds, and unwanted artifacts with simple prompts. Prompt: "Remove the noise from the BG, make the BG white. Remove the pocket outline from the bomber jacket." Instead of trying to solve everything in one huge prompt, I usually make small changes one at a time. It's easier to control the result and understand what each prompt changed. 5. Generate new poses and angles Once the main character design is locked, you can start generating different poses. Find pose references you like and ask the model to reproduce them while keeping the mascot's appearance, anatomy, clothes, and proportions consistent. Prompt: "Create a new pose strictly using the appearance and anatomy of the mascot on the first image. Use the second image as a pose reference. Do not change the clothes of the mascot and his appearance." 6. Build the presentation The final step is to put the mascot into actual design compositions. For this project, I created three posters around the character. This helps prove that the mascot isn't just an isolated AI generation, but part of a visual system that can work across the brand. At this point, you already have a coherent concept you can put in front of a client. You don't necessarily need to build the final production-ready 3D model yourself. These generations can serve as a detailed visual reference for an illustrator, 3D artist, or motion designer who takes the mascot into production (which we often do at @relate_studio. 7. Scaling the approach Once the character is established, you can keep expanding it with new poses, expressions, compositions, environments, and campaign ideas. The important part is locking the character's core visual language first. From there, AI becomes a fast way to explore how the mascot can live across websites, social media, motion, advertising, and other brand materials. You don't need to be an illustrator or 3D designer to explore mascot concepts anymore. You mainly need a strong visual direction, good references, and the ability to judge which outputs are actually worth developing. However, for concepts that you'd like to scale, like we did with Jupiter, it can be helpful to handcraft the mascot after you achieve a great concept About Us @relate_studio is an international, full-cycle design studio. Our portfolio includes Jupiter, Sui, Solana, fomo, Mysten Labs, Crypto.com, and hundreds of other companies. We use AI regularly, but not as a replacement for design thinking. We use it where it saves time without sacrificing quality. If you need help with design, schedule a call at relate.studio.

post.author: Rohan Nayak
post.text:
We grew from ~0 to $500M ARR, adding $250M last year alone while being EBITDA profitable.

1,300-word post on every growth tactic that worked for us:

1. What got us from 0-$400M ARR in the US works in every country.
2. Retention and Monetisation Hacks.
3. Localization > Translation. 4. Experiment with $1M internal seed checks. 5. Pivoting to only AI content production unlocked 100% ARR growth. Pocket FM is like Netflix for audio-only dramas, with our own pool of one-person studios. 1. Acquisition Playbook for 0-$10M ARR in any country in 6 months We run a 90 sec video trailer of an audio drama as an Ad and ask users to download the app if they're interested in the rest of the story. Our core insight after spending >$100M on acquisition is: If the clickthrough rate (CTR) for an ad goes from 2% to 2.25%, our customer acquisition cost (CAC) decreases by ~ 30%. We remodelled our system around this insight and built an AI-first 2.25% CTR ad manufacturing machine that works in every country. For every new country, we take our hit shows -> use LLMs to extract and most intriguing moments -> Write a 5-min script combining all the best parts. The first 60 seconds has to have a hook every 5 seconds and needs to end with a crazy cliffhanger to force a download mid-scroll. If a marketing video is not hitting our benchmarks (2.5% CTR and 55% 3-second through-play), a creative director gets involved to change the hook or cliffhanger to get the numbers there. AI lets us make 1,000 Ads per show, and in total we do ~17.5k Ads per month. When a business creating scales from 1k to 10k Ads, the normal thing is for CAC to skyrocket. But with what I just shared, we 7-8x'd our User Acquisition budget without increasing our CAC materially. It took us 8 months to figure this out, but then the timeline from 0-$10M in every country got shorter and shorter: US revenue grew to $25M in 19 months. (US is now 78% of total) Germany to 21M in 11 months. France to $10M in 3 months. 2. Retention and Monetisation Hacks. We knew we wanted to create an audio entertainment platform, but there was no standard format. For the first 2-3 years, we tried 10 different formats before landing on the winner. After we got it right with audio drama (8-12min chapters, written for mobile fiction, serialized, episodes have strong hooks and end on cliffhangers), avg daily streaming time went from ~25mins to 150+. Audio drama made us realize that Pocket FM was creating a whole new medium. There was no playbook for anything that we were doing. Everything had to be thought & built from scratch. This is what we did for each major bullet: - Monetization: Users have some free daily minutes to listen; then it's pay per episode. We also added the option for users to unlock episodes by watching ads, which is doing extremely well. Ads scaled from zero to a ~$90M run rate in 12 months. - Engagement & production: You don't become obsessed with an app you open once a week. To have users engage daily, we make the next episode free every day. Also helps them build the habit. - Discovery. Huge problem because people consuming Pocket FM enter the app, tap the show, and lock the screen. We fixed it by doing "playlists" of episodes. Once users's free minutes on a show are done, we ask users if they want to pay. If they say no, we play a new show, one where they haven't used their free mins. And we stitch episodes of different shows together that way, creating natural discovery. 3. Localization > translation. 78% of our revenue is still concentrated in the US. Localisation is fixing this: You might write a show for a Spanish audience where language, jokes, folklore, have a certain flavor; if you merely translate the show for, say, a Norwegian audience, that color is lost and hurts the show in the Norway. Quality control is done with LLM as a judge, and LLMs are quite tough. Results are very encouraging: - 12-month revenue retention went from 44% to 76%. - In the past year, we added $250M in net new ARR. __________________________________ Pocket Entertainment (Pocket FM + Pocket Saga) has become the largest AI entertainment platform. We have the largest storytelling catalog with 770,000 titles, 550k creators, and 5.5B hours of playtime with minute by minute retention & engagement data. We are using all of this data to improve every aspect of our business. Our Bet: In the next 3 years we will be able to produce Naruto-like series for $1000. Netflix has to spend $17B to find 100 Blockbusters per year. What happens when you can produce 1M high quality shows for $1B? The streaming wars caused a $300B reallocation of market cap. The AI entertainment wars may be a $1T+ reshuffling of market cap. We are at a unique spot. Unlike other AI creator tools like Runway or Midjourney, we own both the supply and demand side of AI content. post.author: alexei
post.text: Somewhere out there is a version of you that's wealthier, calmer, more confident, better with people, more disciplined, less afraid. And here's the part almost nobody explains properly: the gap between you and that person isn't talent, luck, or genetics. It's wiring. Literal, physical wiring inside your skull. And wiring can change. That's neuroplasticity. Once you actually understand how it works, you stop seeing it as a cute science fact and start seeing it for what it is: the single mechanism sitting underneath every transformation a human being has ever made. Every person who went from broke to wealthy, anxious to calm, weak to strong, undisciplined to relentless, did it through this exact process, whether they knew the name for it or not. And the same mechanism, running in reverse, is why people stay stuck in the exact patterns that are ruining their lives. Same tool. Opposite outcomes. It just depends on what you feed it. The Century Science Got Wrong For most of the 1900s, the accepted scientific position was brutal: the adult brain was finished. You got a certain number of neurons, you slowly lost them, and whatever wiring you had by your twenties was basically your ceiling for life. Early neuroanatomists like Santiago Ramón y Cajal, the man who laid the groundwork for modern neuroscience, believed that in a mature brain, once damaged, connections simply couldn't come back. That line got treated as gospel for decades. Doctors told stroke patients to accept whatever function they had left. Teachers assumed the "slow" seven year old would be a slow adult. An entire century of medicine, education, and self-improvement got built on top of an assumption that turned out to be flat wrong. Hints of the truth showed up way earlier than people realize. Philosopher William James floated the idea of an adaptable brain all the way back in 1890. But it had no name and no proof, just a hunch. The term "neural plasticity" wasn't formally coined until 1948, by Polish neuroscientist Jerzy Konorski. A year later, psychologist Donald Hebb published the line that would become neuroscience's most repeated sentence: neurons that fire together, wire together. Hebb had handed the field its first real theory of how learning physically happens in the brain, decades before the scanning technology existed to prove he was right. It took until brain imaging finally caught up, late in the 20th century and into the 21st, for neuroplasticity to go from fringe idea to accepted fact. The old "fixed brain" model didn't collapse because someone argued it into the ground. It collapsed because scientists started scanning real brains and watching them change in real time. What Neuroplasticity Actually Is Neuroplasticity is your brain's ability to physically reorganize itself, structurally and functionally, for your entire life. Not a metaphor. Not a self-help buzzword wearing a lab coat. When you learn something, practice a skill, recover from injury, or change a habitual thought, real physical changes happen inside your head. New connections form between neurons. Existing ones get stronger or weaker. In certain regions, entirely new neurons get born. And here's the part that matters most: this happens whether you're paying attention or not. Every skill you have, every habit you've built, every fear you carry, is neuroplasticity already at work. Your brain doesn't care if the wiring serves you or wrecks you. It just responds to repetition. That's the whole game, and it's why this is a cheat code rather than a nice fact. You already have the tool. The only question is whether you're using it on purpose. The Mechanics: How the Rewiring Actually Happens Three processes do the heavy lifting. Synaptic plasticity is the moment to moment layer. Connections between neurons, called synapses, get stronger with repeated use through a process called long-term potentiation, and weaker with disuse through long-term depression. This is the direct biological basis of "practice makes permanent." Fire a pathway once, it's easier to fire again. Fire it a thousand times, it becomes close to automatic. Structural plasticity is slower and shows up on an actual scan. Neurons physically grow new branches, called dendrites, to connect with other neurons, or prune away branches they no longer use. Do something long enough and the brain literally reshapes the physical real estate devoted to it. Neurogenesis, the birth of brand new neurons, was once believed to stop entirely after childhood. It doesn't. Research shows it continues in specific regions of the adult brain, especially the hippocampus, the structure central to memory and spatial learning. When this was first discovered it directly contradicted a century of dogma about a fixed number of neurons, and a lot of scientists didn't want to believe it. Together these three processes mean your brain is never a finished product. It's a permanent construction site, and you're the foreman, whether you show up to manage the site or not. The Proof Isn't Theoretical. It's On Brain Scans. This isn't abstract. It's measured, photographed, and compared against control groups. The famous case is London's taxi drivers. To get licensed, they have to pass a brutal exam called "The Knowledge," memorizing roughly 25,000 streets and thousands of landmarks, a process that takes years. Researchers scanned their brains and found something wild: their hippocampi, the region tied to spatial memory, were measurably larger than in non-drivers. The longer someone had been driving, the bigger the difference. Their brains physically grew around the demand placed on them. Musicians show something similar. Studies on professional string players found expanded regions of the sensory cortex mapped to the fingers of the left hand, the hand doing the intricate fingering work on a violin or cello neck. Years of deliberate repetition reshaped the brain's own internal map of the body. And the most powerful evidence comes from rehab clinics. Stroke patients using a treatment called constraint-induced movement therapy have their unaffected limb deliberately restrained, forcing the brain to reroute motor function through the damaged side. Patients have regained real motor function years after doctors told them recovery had plateaued. The brain didn't just cope with the damage. It built a new map around it. The Part Nobody Tells You: You Can Grow Willpower Like a Muscle Here's where this stops being trivia and starts being personal. There's a small region deep in your brain called the anterior midcingulate cortex. Neuroscientist Andrew Huberman and former Navy SEAL David Goggins broke down the research on it in a conversation that's since traveled everywhere, and the finding is almost too good to be true: this region physically grows when you do things you don't want to do. Not things you enjoy. Not things that come easy. The tasks that create friction. Resisting a temptation. Forcing yourself through a workout you dread. Sticking with a diet when the craving hits. Studies cited in that conversation show this brain region is measurably smaller in people who consistently avoid discomfort, and measurably larger in athletes, people who've pushed through serious adversity, and people who live unusually long. It's also linked to preventing the kind of cognitive decline that shows up later in life. Older adults who perform exceptionally well on cognitive testing tend to have a larger version of this same structure. Goggins put it about as plainly as it can be put: there's no hack for this. No shortcut. You build it the same way you build any muscle, by loading it with resistance over and over until it adapts. The "suck" isn't a side effect of building willpower. It's the mechanism. This is the part that should genuinely change how you see your own potential. Confidence, discipline, grit, the ability to keep showing up when everything in you wants to quit, none of that is a fixed personality trait some people are born with and others aren't. It's a muscle with a name and a location, and it responds to training exactly like any other muscle does. The Chemical Switch That Turns Learning On There's a second piece from that same research world worth knowing, because it's immediately usable. Huberman has explained that adult neuroplasticity depends heavily on a brain chemical called acetylcholine, released from a structure called the nucleus basalis. Acetylcholine is what opens the biological "window" that makes new learning possible. Without enough of it, your brain can be sitting right in front of new information and barely absorb any of it. The practical hack: brief, high-intensity physical movement triggers a release of acetylcholine and norepinephrine that creates a sharp, alert, focused state, the exact state your brain needs to be in for rewiring to happen efficiently. This is part of why people who exercise before or during a learning session often retain more than people who sit still the whole time. It's also why, according to this research, doing focused learning in the few hours after intense exercise (not exhausted, just alert) tends to work better than trying to learn while flat and sluggish. Sleep matters just as much on the back end, since a large portion of the actual structural rewiring gets consolidated while you're asleep. Put those two together and you get an actual protocol, not a vague suggestion: move hard for a few minutes, then learn or practice the thing you're trying to build, then protect your sleep that night. That's not motivational poster advice. That's the chemistry. Why Struggle Is the Point, Not the Obstacle Neuroscientist Lara Boyd, who studies stroke recovery and neuroplasticity at the University of British Columbia, has made a point that upends how most people think about learning: the more you struggle while practicing a skill, the more your brain physically changes and the more you actually learn. Comfortable, easy repetition barely moves the needle. Practice that pushes you past your comfort zone drives real structural change. This also explains why cookie cutter advice so often falls flat. Because people's brains are wired differently based on their individual history, the same instruction or the same recovery protocol can work beautifully for one person and do almost nothing for another. That's not a flaw in the science. It's the whole point. Personalized effort beats generic effort, every time. The Simplest Way to Picture What's Happening All of this gets abstract fast, so it helps to have one clean image in your head. A widely used explainer describes the brain as a dynamic, connected power grid, with billions of pathways lighting up every time you think, feel, or act. When you think about something differently, learn a new task, or choose a different emotional response, you're carving a new road through that grid. Travel that road enough times and your brain starts favoring it. The new way of thinking or doing becomes the default, while the old pathway, used less and less, gradually fades. That's the entire mechanism in one image: new roads get built through repetition, old ones decay through neglect. It's a simplification obviously, real neurons don't look like a highway map, but it lines up cleanly with the actual biology. Synaptic strengthening is the road getting wider and faster. Disuse-driven weakening is the road falling apart from lack of traffic. This framing has traveled far past neuroscience classrooms. It's used in chronic pain treatment to explain why persistent pain can become a kind of learned pathway that outlives the original injury, and why that same plasticity can also unwind it. It's used in workplace safety training to explain how repeated unsafe habits get grooved into automatic behavior, and how practicing safer routines on purpose can replace them. The Case That Shows Just How Far This Goes If you want a real jaw drop, consider a case out of China that circulated widely in neuroscience circles. A woman in her twenties was admitted to a hospital after complaining of dizziness and nausea. Scans revealed something almost unheard of: she had lived her entire life without a cerebellum, the part of the brain responsible for balance, coordinated movement, and parts of speech. She walked a little unsteadily, her speech was mildly affected, but she had gotten married, held a job, and raised a child, all without a structure doctors consider essential for basic motor function. What filled the gap was neuroplasticity. Other regions of her brain had spent decades quietly rerouting around the missing structure, taking on jobs they were never originally built for. It's an extreme example, and nobody is claiming you can casually build a whole new "you" the way her brain built a workaround for a missing cerebellum. But it's a genuinely useful data point for just how far the brain's rerouting capacity can stretch when it has no other option. If a brain missing an entire structure can still find a way to function, the wiring standing between you and the version of yourself you want to become is a much smaller problem than it feels like at 11pm when you're deciding whether to hit snooze again. Why "I'm Just Built This Way" Doesn't Hold Up Anymore Almost everyone has a sentence like this somewhere in their head. I'm just not a numbers person. I've always been anxious. I've never had discipline. That's just who I am. Neuroplasticity doesn't erase the fact that these patterns are real and often feel completely involuntary. It does something more useful: it reclassifies them. Every one of those sentences is describing your brain's current wiring, built through years of repetition you mostly didn't choose on purpose. It was built by whatever you were exposed to, whatever you practiced by accident, whatever got reinforced by your environment, your fears, or your habits. None of that makes it permanent. It just makes it the wiring you happen to have right now. This is a genuinely different way to relate to your own limitations. Instead of "that's just my personality," it becomes "that's the pathway I've reinforced the most." One of those is a life sentence. The other is a maintenance problem, and maintenance problems have solutions. Wealth, confidence, discipline, calm under pressure, none of these are handed out at birth to a lucky few. They're the observable output of specific pathways getting strengthened over specific periods of time through specific repeated behavior. Anyone willing to put in that repetition is working with the same biological toolkit as the people who already have what they want. The Uncomfortable Part: This Cuts Both Directions Neuroplasticity doesn't have a moral compass. It doesn't care whether what you're repeating is good for you. Anxious spirals, procrastination, self-doubt, doom scrolling, every time you run one of those loops you are, in a very literal biological sense, training your brain to run it faster and easier next time. The exact mechanism that grows a taxi driver's hippocampus is the mechanism strengthening whatever pattern you keep repeating, good or bad. There's a quote from Huberman worth sitting with here: at the end of the day, the only thing you can truly control is where you place your attention and where you place your effort. That's it. That's the entire lever. Not motivation, not talent, not luck. Attention and effort, repeated, become wiring. Wiring becomes identity. Identity becomes your life. How to Actually Use This Knowing the mechanism only matters if it changes what you do. Here's the practical version, grounded directly in the biology above: - Frequency beats intensity. Because synaptic strengthening depends on repeated activation, short and consistent practice reliably beats rare marathon sessions. Five focused minutes daily will outbuild one exhausted three hour session a week. - Load the resistance on purpose. If you want to build real willpower, stop looking for a hack and start doing the specific thing you don't want to do. That discomfort is the input the anterior midcingulate cortex is designed to respond to. - Move before you learn. Short bursts of intense movement prime your brain chemically for the learning that follows. Use that window instead of ignoring it. - Protect your sleep. Structural rewiring gets locked in while you're asleep. Cutting sleep while trying to build a skill is fighting your own biology. - Interrupt the loops you don't want. Rumination and self-criticism strengthen the same way any other pathway does. Catching the loop and redirecting it, even imperfectly, weakens it a little more each time. - Expect proportional timelines. Undoing a two week old habit and undoing a twenty year old pattern are not the same task biologically. Both are possible. Neither happens overnight, and expecting instant results is one of the most common reasons people quit right before the change would have taken hold. A Few Myths Worth Killing Neuroplasticity does not mean you can rewire your brain overnight through sheer willpower alone. The mechanisms above, synaptic strengthening, structural remodeling, neurogenesis, take sustained repetition over weeks and months, not a single motivated Monday. It also doesn't mean your brain is infinitely malleable at every age in the exact same way. Plasticity is highest in early childhood and takes more deliberate effort as you get older, but "more effort required" is a world away from "impossible," which is what the old model claimed. The Real Takeaway Here's the uncomfortable truth hiding underneath all of this: your brain is being shaped right now, today, by whatever you're repeating, on purpose or completely by accident. Neuroplasticity isn't a special power reserved for elite athletes or Navy SEALs or people doing intensive cognitive training. It's simply how the organ works, constantly, in the background, whether you're steering it or not. The taxi driver didn't set out to grow a bigger hippocampus. The musician didn't consciously decide to expand their sensory cortex. Both outcomes were side effects of repetition aimed at something else entirely. That's the real cheat code hiding inside the science. You don't need to understand the neurobiology to benefit from it. You just need to be deliberate about what you repeat, because your brain is going to rebuild itself around it either way, whether that's the version of you who's wealthy, confident, and disciplined, or the version stuck exactly where they are. The tool was never missing. It's been running this whole time. The only real choice you get is whether the repetition is intentional. I hope that was helpful enough to get you started. post.author: Paul Klay
post.text: I’ve never had a normal job and now I’m writing an article about how to easily get a good one but even though I’ve never had a normal job, I have something much more valuable: after being an influencer and building a couple of successful startups, I started joining new projects as a cofounder and I’m not talking about random early-stage startups. I mean projects that were already pretty well known for example, I became a cofounder of a cartoon that’s been around for 16 years and has 3M+ followers and in a pretty similar way, I became a partner at Begin Capital so I want to share the main principles that helped me get into these positions they can help you gain valuable experience much faster, get access to much bigger opportunities, and make some money along the way 1. why I wouldn’t apply for jobs through standard application forms there’s a logical reason for this, and there’s research backing it up when a founder is hiring, their job is to find the best possible person for the role but no matter how good your hiring process is, figuring out how good someone actually is takes time interviews only tell you so much. eventually you need to see the person work that’s why referrals and people you already know are so valuable someone has already worked with them, seen what they can do, and validated them over time the risk is much lower also, great specialists usually aren’t actively looking for jobs if you’re really good at what you do and consistently make money for businesses, people eventually know about you and when they need someone with your skill set, they’ll come to you your goal is to get into that category once you do, both your chances and the quality of opportunities you get become much better so how do you get there? 2. clearly understand your strengths “I can do everything” isn’t an answer you could reframe it as: “I have a lot of time and I’m willing to spend it” not a bad start but you still need to spend that time doing something useful for whoever you want to work with look at what you do best what’s your strongest skill? what’s something specific about you that people remember? an easy way to figure this out is to ask people who have actually worked with you but ask the right questions “am I good at marketing?” is an incredibly bad question you’re basically asking them to validate something you already believe ask open-ended questions instead: “what stood out to you about working with me?” “when did you feel like I handled something particularly well?” “what do you think I’m unusually good at?” let people tell you what they actually think you should eventually end up with 1–3 things that genuinely differentiate you and that you do better than most people you can go even further if you have multiple hypotheses about your strengths, test them see which one resonates most with people and creates the most interest 3. clearly understand who actually needs your strengths being great at something doesn’t automatically make you valuable to every company imagine you’re insanely good at building viral consumer products that could be an incredibly valuable skill for a consumer startup but if you walk into an HFT firm and pitch them the exact same skill, they might have absolutely no use for it the skill didn’t become less valuable you’re just talking to the wrong company so once you understand what you’re good at, the next step is figuring out exactly who needs it this is roughly how I think about it: start with your strongest skill figure out what result that skill can produce for a company then figure out how that result eventually turns into money after that, look for industries and products where this is especially valuable and finally, find companies that need it but aren’t doing it well yet you should be able to look at a company and build a very simple case in your head: “you’re building X” “right now, you’re missing Y” “I looked at the market and Y seems to be working really well for companies like A, B and C” “if it works for you, it could have a meaningful impact on revenue” “I know how to build Y because I’ve already done Z” “here are the results” that’s the level of clarity you want before you ever reach out you should understand exactly why this company needs what you’re good at and how your work could eventually turn into money for them 4. how to do outreach at this point you might be thinking: Paul, this all sounds great. obviously I need to be useful but how do I actually get a great job? you need to reach the founder this probably won’t work the same way with huge corporations, so I’d focus on promising startups you’ll probably get more experience, build better connections, and have much more upside if the company succeeds you can meet founders: on X in relevant communities and niche groups through mutual connections ideally, you want a warm intro I explained how to get one here: https://x.com/PaulKlayVC/status/2095544871457059136?s=20 roughly the same concept works with founders 5. how to build the relationship once you know which founders you want to meet and how to reach them, you need to figure out what to actually say treat it as a mix of getting to know someone and making a sale but make it as natural and non-pushy as possible I’d start by asking for advice while making it clear that the conversation could be interesting for them as well something like: “hey! i’m Paul, Venture Partner at Begin Capital and ex-cofounder of ... been looking into ... recently and found a couple of things that seem to work really well in this market wanted to chat with someone who actually knows the space and see what i might be missing would love to get your take” now you have a reason to talk that doesn’t sound like: “hey, can you give me a job?” once they agree to a call, go deeper explain why you became interested in the market and show that you actually did your homework then start asking questions around the opportunity you found for example: “I went through most of the competitors and noticed that a lot of them are doing X and Y. from what I can see, it seems to be working extremely well” “you guys aren’t really doing it right now. is there a specific reason?” listen to the answer maybe they already tried it maybe it didn’t work maybe there’s something about the market you didn’t understand or maybe they’ll say: “yeah, we’ve actually thought about this before, we just never had the time to do it” perfect keep digging show them the cases you found, explain why you think the opportunity is interesting, and walk through how it could eventually turn into money but there’s one important thing I wouldn’t do on the first call: don’t immediately say: “I can do this for you” that makes the whole conversation feel like a disguised job pitch you want the founder to understand the opportunity first ideally, by the end of the conversation, they should already be thinking: “shit, maybe we actually should be doing this” that’s where I’d stop don’t try to close anything right away give them some time to think about the opportunity and start looking for ways to execute it themselves if the opportunity is real and you explained it well, there’s a good chance they’ll realize they either don’t have the right person for it or simply don’t have the time and now they already know someone who understands the problem, has done the research, and has relevant experience you that’s a much better position than trying to sell yourself from minute one and that brings us to the most important part 6. prove your maximum value with almost zero risk for the person hiring you your job is to make saying yes as easy as possible if you’re confident in your abilities and genuinely good at what you’re talking about, prove it offer something like: “I’d be interested in testing the hypotheses we discussed you have the right product and I already have experience with this let me try it if it works, everyone makes money and we scale it if it doesn’t, you lose almost nothing and still get the hypothesis tested” that’s it most of the risk is on you because you’re the one who needs the opportunity in the first place and if everything you said actually makes sense, the founder now has very little reason to say no from their perspective, it should sound something like this: some guy showed up everything he’s saying makes sense, and we’ve actually thought about some of it before we just never had the time to execute he has relevant experience and cases and now he’s willing to prove that it works without asking for much upfront why does that arrangement make sense for you? because you might have the skill, but you don’t have the product where you can apply it building the entire product yourself could take years and require a completely different set of skills instead, you can use someone else’s existing product and distribution to prove that your skill actually creates value maybe you make the company $5,000 and get paid $2,000 you made money they made money you gained experience you built a real case study and now you have a much stronger position to keep working with them or do the same thing with another company without that company, you might never have had the opportunity to generate that $5,000 in the first place, even if you were genuinely good at what you do win-win obviously, not everyone will agree to this but trust me, your odds are much better than sending the same CV through 100 application forms and even when it doesn’t immediately turn into a job, you’re building experience, relationships, reputation, and case studies all of that compounds over time move faster and smarter than everyone else there are way fewer rules and boundaries than you think if you’re actually good and know how to create value

One of the best businesses to build with Jev is a local services matcher.

It's a form with a classifier behind it. 

Someone types what they need, and they get matched with a company near them before they close the tab.

post.author: Dhravya Shah
post.text: Instinct has taken the world by storm over the last two weeks - it's one of the best imessage assistants I've used. as with every product, I decided to reverse-engineer Instinct's memory to find out exactly how it works. I've been working on agent memory for the last 3 years, and the founder of @supermemory. The industry is constantly changing and there's no right answer to "how to do agent memory". Each product has different needs and constraints! Surprisingly, instinct's memory aligns with our views of memory, and you can fully replicate it with supermemory (how-to in the end) because I've been doing this for so long, I have somewhat of a good intuition of how memory systems typically work, so I can reverse-engineer memory systems by just probing on the surface of the agent (imessage interface) This is gonna be a bit long! Instinct is powered by git-tracked markdown files. At it's core, the memories are stored as git-tracked markdown files, BUT with a lot of harness specific engineering done to make it seamless and fast. The answering model (Likely an open-weights model) receives: Current conversation context an identity "profile" of the user a memory one-pager (of what's going on) a compaction recap and a to-do / Tasks board We were able to reconstruct and gather this evidence by a lot of probing with questions and navigating through general assumptions, and then trying to verify them. Most of the things here should be very correct here, but because i haven't seen their code, some things may be wrong. Apart from the files, Instinct has about 4,250 tokens of somewhat of a "profile" and ~10k tokens of compacted conversation context (which, obv, depends on the conversation) So let's start there! Profile and memory one-pager A profile is essentially a gist of what the model _always_ needs to know about the user. Instinct's profile has: Life context: a summary of selected user circumstances and relevant people or work. Autonomy calibration: selected preferences about when the assistant should act or ask. Channel communication style: selected preferences about how to communicate. These are the "headers" that instinct sees. PS: Supermemory has profiles built in, https://supermemory.ai/docs/concepts/user-profiles and has the same learnings, we split it into static and dynamic parts of the profile. How are these profiles formed? The best-supported reconstruction I could find here, is a derived summary of saved records. We do not know whether the generator reads all files, changed files, search results, earlier summaries, or independently stored facts. The generator (Or dreaming, learning) model, prompt, scheduling, conflict handling and response to forget requests remain unknown. A complete one-pager backing file was not found in the agent’s accessible copy; that does not establish where it is actually stored. So, this profile is likely not a file, but just an ad-hoc created cache of sorts. This profile is also not kept very fresh. In some cases, I was able to find a 2-day profile lag, but because there's dates in it, the agent is able to assume that it's not fully trustable. In supermemory, the profiles are formed automatically and always kept fresh The file and folders Now, let's come to the file structure that instinct uses. In my few days of using it, here's the file structure it came up with: I was able to find a lot of redundant, stale, or duplicate information, but that likely just helps the agent find the answer better. Instinct reported that commit 899f88a added the preference to a communications digest, daily timeline, and dining note. The README described raw, hourly, and monthly timeline tiers, but those directories were absent from its accessible copy. File structures Files reportedly use structured headers followed by prose and bullets. This is an illustrative example: A few things stand out from the file structure: Files have names, but also IDs. There's about 4 types, in my account: preference, person, organization, and conversation Information itself is in the form of a list of facts (despite it being in a file) [[links]] connect related files, by ID. So yes, it's a densely interconnected set of files, and the links make it graph-like. Aliases are included, we'll get to why in the harness specific stuff later. Creating, updating, organizing info It seems like the reconciliation commits do more than just append information: Move temporary details into workstreams. Shorten durable records while linking to fuller notes. Turn examples into broader traits. Remove incidental details. Replace incorrect facts with dated corrections Versioning Old information can remain in Git history. It can also remain in a dated note even after a current fact file changes. This info can only be brought back if the model explicitly looks for older versions. supermemory's ingestion works in a similar way, and done by a specialized model! Also, we automatically include old versions, so the model doesn't have to look for them. Forgetting Instinct does forget things based on when the ingestion runs etc. But, this is not "automatic" right now. So, an explicit "This is not happening" _will_ be forgotten, but "I have my exams this weekend" will remain in the records (unless the model looks at it and chooses to remove it) Supermemory has forgetfulness embedded into the system. So, things automatically forget and evolve, instead of an agent having to do it. When does ingestion / this work even happen? Right now, the ingestion works once every 24 hours. (I'm assuming, because a preference took approximately 23 hours 16 minutes from message to reported commit). BTW If you text Instinct too much in 24 hours, it will quite literally tell you to come back tomorrow (Since you can't compact beyond a certain token threshold) So it's likely a cron job running every day to maintain the set of files, and edit the current ones. Harness - Bringing memory to the agent Ok, so now we know how instinct actually put the files arranges the files and stuff. But, how is the agent actually using this info? There's no vector indexing, or BM25 search. Instinct quite literally just uses keyword matching / grep-style queries to look things up in the file system. This is why every file has aliases associated, so that every file has a good chance of showing up when the agent is looking for it. I found out by running multiple different queries in different ways. Full structure Instinct seems to be using bash-like tools to do Grep, list, inspect git, and a few tools to manage it's TODO list. At the start of the conversation, a profile is injected Instinct makes use of the tools available to look up more information. A part of the profile is an index for the available things. Memory is read only, atleast for the agent. This is something I'm personally a big believer in, actually! A background process does the work of combining things, not the main agent. Performance of instinct's memory It's hard to benchmark from the agent surface, but here's my vibe-test rubrik for instinct's memory: Single-fact recall: ✅ Multi-hop across sessions: Weak ☑️ Temporal / recency: ✅ Update & contradiction: ✅ Abstention: ✅ Forgetting / decay: Partial: Automatic forgetting missing. Pruning present Performance at >1M tokens or months: Untested but good vibes☑️ Procedural / skill memory: ❌ Not present (None of the memories we could find were directional) Test-time learning: ✅ Corrected behavior within conversation; durable learning unverified Implicit Personalization: ❌ ("buy me a monitor" -> it should know I'm a founder, new office, etc. and suggest premium choices) Explicit Personalization: ✅ Multimodal: ❌ Weak ('you know how my room looks. what colored blankets should I buy?') Write-side cost: ☑️ Likely expensive, but untestable. We know that writes will get exponentially more expensive for the agent to work through, as it has to READ through current info to WRITE more info (and consolidate and manage things). This should be fine for personal agent use case, we're not sure yet! Overall: capable under explicit retrieval instructions, inconsistent in natural personalization, with forgetting guarantees unresolved. Really really good! Implementing it with supermemory There's some benefits of using supermemory here, and it is actually super obvious to implement! Buckets for entities and relationships: Supermemory supports Profile Buckets. Each user can get their own set of buckets, which is dynamic. This is like having a folder of info that the LLM can access. https://supermemory.ai/docs/user-profiles/buckets Profile at the start of the conversation Supermemory has a profile system built in, so that would be included at the start Search tools Give the agent search tools, with a few specific options like including forgetted and history of memories, in case if it needs those! https://supermemory.ai/docs/api-reference/recall-search/search-memory-entries Ingest every 1-day conversation Instinct-like interface would run `memories.add()` every turn, with the current day being the ID of the conversation. Supermemory's ingestion automatically handles forgetfulness, reconciliation, and conflict resolution. https://supermemory.ai/docs/concepts/graph-memory#dreaming-keeps-the-graph-alive Supermemory also automatically handles multi-modal ingestion! Below would the full Instinct memory system that works, in supermemory ~exactly like instinct. Just 60 lines of code!!!!! supermemory is specialized towards memory (duh), so it is much cheaper to run, much faster, while being fully composable at the same time. Instead of Git, we have our own versioning system that's embedded with our data structure. Instead of full files, we construct files 'on-demand' which also makes sure that info is always fresh. https://x.com/DhravyaShah/status/2101535378557874196?s=20 So yes, that's how Instinct's memory works, and how can implement instinct's memory system with supermemory completely!

post.author: Ben Cera
post.text: When I launched Polsia in December 2025, it was crickets. Nobody knew the product existed. Today, over 25,000 people pay for it. But every stage between those two numbers needed a different playbook. And if you run them in the wrong order, you waste time and money. Here’s every step, in order: ↓↓↓ The idea Before you validate anything, you need to know the idea is worth building. My test is simple. You have the idea, and the next morning you wake up still thinking it’s good. Then for 5-7 days afterwards, you keep thinking it’s good. If it passes that test, it’s probably an idea worth building. But then you need to decide if you’re willing to dedicate the next 5 years to it. Everyone’s answer is different. The validation You can validate an idea before you build a single thing. Create a landing page with an email waitlist and a Typeform. Then run Meta ads and send that traffic to the page. What you’re watching for is whether a stranger who sees your ad will leave their email, finish the entire form, and tell you why they’re interested. That gives you a lot of signal on whether you should build it. So if you can’t get anyone to do that, move to the next idea. This is how I validated Polsia. My Typeform asked people how much autonomy they’d want from an AI, and how much they’d be willing to pay for it. The responses were amazing. The first 10 customers I learned how to get first customers from Travis Kalanick at CloudKitchens. I had built a service to help restaurants with their digital marketing, and I told Travis there were millions of restaurants who could use it. Then I asked him if I could hire a salesperson. He said. “Trust me, you don’t want to scale something that doesn’t work. You’re the salesperson. Go sign up 10 restaurants and prove it works.” So I started calling restaurants myself. Including ones already operating out of our kitchens. A week later, I came back with 10 restaurants, and he let me hire a salesperson. The lesson? Your first 10 paying customers come from hustlin’. The signal So how many customers do you need before you’ve found product-market-fit? 1 paying customer is a good start. 10 means you’re on the right track. Then once you’re at 100 active, happy, paying customers who stay for 2-3 months, you probably found product-market-fit. But even that’s not true product-market-fit. To me, you’ve found it when you can profitably grow a use case at scale, and whatever that looks like depends on your business model. The product Between 10-100 customers, focus on improving the product. Knowing how to get customers is a good skill, but scaling something that doesn’t work is a waste of time and money. Wait until you understand your customer and know you’re adding value. That’s why I barely touched my pre-seed before I found product-market-fit. Having capital doesn’t mean you should spend it. It means you should reserve it for the moment you’re ready to scale. The biggest product fix I made was onboarding. The first version of Polsia was email-based. You’d give it your email and get a daily update on the work done, which meant the wow moment was delayed until they checked their emails. I realized people had to see the experience first. So now, in the first few minutes of onboarding, Polsia researches your idea and starts building the company in front of you. Only then does it ask you to start a free trial. The faster your user hits the wow moment, the more users will pay. The price Charge enough to recoup your money at some point and be profitable. When I priced Polsia, I added up what one customer cost me. The AI runs on task every night, which came out to about $30 in AI costs. On top of that, a web server with a database cost me $5 to $10 a month, and I embed API keys so customers never have to think about them. That got me to roughly $50. So I charged $49 a month plus 20% of the revenue their business made. I roughly broke even on the subscription and made money when they made money. You can also be smart about where your costs are heading. I bet AI costs would come down, and once I cut my AI bill by running open-source models on rented GPUs, I could afford to offer a free version. Some companies right now don’t charge anything at all. But unless you’re really viral, I think that’s pretty irresponsible. Because eventually you will have to charge and free users might leave. The scale Before product-market-fit, hustling on X and online is enough. Once you have a business model and retention, hit every channel, all the time. When I had a couple hundred users, I knew it was time to put fuel on the fire so I moved to SF and did my marketing stunt… Having Polsia raise my $30 million round. Nothing beats putting effort into marketing and product, it compounds. The conclusion A great product with no marketing gets you zero users, or very slow growth. Great storytelling with a bad product gets you attention, but no growth. And a great product with great storytelling will make you successful. This process gets harder at every stage. But if you’re consistent and follow this guide, 25,000 customers is inevitable. Try Polsia here: polsia.com

title: Learn by Copy
tldr: Jason Cohen argues that copying other writers' style, not their words, is a practical way to discover your own voice and strengths as a writer.

highlights.text: High School English III doesn't teach you how to write prose in the real world any more than a college CS degree teaches you how to write code in the real world.
Rather, copying is one of the best ways of learning, growing, evaluating, and exploring. It's a valid tool so long as we regard it as a means to an end.
The goal is to learn and grow as a writer, and this was fun to do.
Copying ironically helps you discover yourself: The way to discovering who you are, what you value, what you're good at, what you believe, is to try things on, like clothes, to see what fits.

excerpt: In America we're trained that all copying is bad; of course plagiarism is, but perhaps we're throwing the baby out with the bathwater.
note: Jason Cohen makes the case for copying structure and style—not words—as a practical way to discover your own strengths and learn how to write.
